description: Width tiers for Languages — F-10 sequence, Year 9-10 band. All standards are capability descriptors. C strand standards use task_contexts as the primary width axis. U strand standards use phenomena_contexts (Systems of language and Language and culture). At this band students operate in familiar and unfamiliar contexts, evaluate and synthesise across sources, interpret cultural meaning, and reflect on identity critically.
subject: Languages

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest single task context or phenomenon that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For C strand: minimum is the narrowest communicative context in which the described extended interaction, contribution, evaluation or creation is genuine — not a simplified or scaffolded version of the task. For U strand: minimum is engagement with the described complex grammatical structure or critical cultural analysis in at least one context.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in elaboration cases. For C strand: a range of task types and communicative contexts — familiar and unfamiliar — reflecting the descriptor's full scope including evaluation, synthesis and perspective-taking. For U strand: the range of complex structures, metalanguage analysis and critical cultural reflection described in the elaborations.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new communicative contexts, cultural communities, linguistic phenomena or analytical frameworks. Width adds breadth of context — not difficulty of the same task. For U strand: additional phenomena, critical perspectives, or comparative cultural frameworks that deepen understanding.
width_notes.elaborations: Target language (F-10 sequence) elaborations were used as the primary source. All target-language-specific vocabulary and grammar examples have been genericised. Elaborations are preserved verbatim in each standard entry as source record.

AC9LS10C01.minimum_width: Initiate and sustain an exchange in at least one unfamiliar context; use at least one discussion strategy (following up on a contribution, maintaining thread, requesting elaboration).
AC9LS10C01.typical_width: Initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts — applying appropriate register across varied situations, exchanging views on topical issues, developing narrative and discussion skills, using structured argument language, interacting in role-plays about travel and services, and participating in discussion using turn-taking and viewpoint strategies.
wider: Participate in a discussion on a genuinely contested topic — arguing a position, responding to counterarguments, and revising a stated view in response to a compelling contribution
Interact in role-play in an unfamiliar scenario (e.g. lost property, service complaint) without preparation — applying available language to a genuinely open-outcome situation
Exchange views with a target language community peer on a topic of mutual interest — adapting language and cultural references appropriately for the audience
elaborations: applying appropriate register and modifying behaviour, language and etiquette in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
exchanging messages with peers in a target language context to share views about aspects of teenage life
interviewing class members to elicit opinions on personal experiences and significant events
maintaining and extending conversations by following up on others' contributions
using language to achieve different purposes in interactions, including contractions and slang for speed and economy
interacting in role-plays or spontaneous skits about travelling and service situations
playing a true and false game relating to past experiences, future aspirations or topics of interest
participating in a discussion, exchanging different viewpoints using strategies such as sentence starters, asking for repetition or inviting elaboration

AC9LS10C02.minimum_width: Contribute at least one reasoned position and respond to at least one different view in a discussion or negotiation; reach or contribute to a shared decision.
AC9LS10C02.typical_width: Contribute to discussions involving diverse views — taking turns, expressing agreement and disagreement, negotiating arrangements and reaching shared decisions, participating in transactions, collaborating on media or broadcast projects using appropriate presentational language, and using argument and persuasive language for topical issues.
wider: Facilitate a class discussion on a topical issue — managing turn-taking, summarising contributions, and steering toward a shared outcome
Participate in a collaborative broadcast or media project — taking genuine responsibility for a content segment and presenting to a real audience
Negotiate a genuinely contested decision (e.g. event planning with competing constraints) — demonstrating that the outcome reflects real compromise across different positions
elaborations: interacting in class discussion and debates by taking turns, expressing agreement/disagreement and providing encouragement
negotiating arrangements, weighing up alternatives and reaching shared decisions in relation to planned activities
participating in real or simulated transactions such as exchanging, ordering and bargaining for consumer items
participating in collaborative projects such as a segment for a community radio or television program
using argument and expressive or persuasive language to discuss topical issues

AC9LS10C03.minimum_width: Evaluate at least one text for perspective, fact/opinion distinction or reliability; synthesise information from at least two sources into a coherent response.
AC9LS10C03.typical_width: Evaluate and synthesise information, ideas and perspectives across a broad range of texts — comparing perspectives on issues, distinguishing fact from opinion, applying for opportunities in the target language, listening to First Nations Australian stories and creating profiles in the target language, summarising and presenting information from multiple sources, adapting texts for different contexts and audiences, and expressing evaluative responses to creative texts.
wider: Compare two conflicting perspectives on an environmental or social issue from target language community sources — synthesise both into a multimodal text that presents the tension fairly
Evaluate a target language community media text (news, social media, advertisement) for perspective and bias — present findings to the class with specific evidence
Create a profile of a First Nations Australian author or storyteller in the target language — drawing on the author's story as source and reflecting on the cultural significance of the work
elaborations: comparing different perspectives about an issue from different stakeholder viewpoints and incorporating information into a multimodal text
exploring persuasive and informative texts to recognise fact versus opinion and presenting findings
reading an advertisement and responding appropriately, addressing key criteria
listening to or reading First Nations Australians' stories in English and creating a profile in the target language
summarising information from sources regarding an issue of interest, determining most important information and presenting with personal perspective
locating and researching information from reliable sources to inform decisions
synthesising information from a range of sources to group and present ideas in a logical manner
adapting and changing texts to suit different contexts, purposes and audiences
analysing published accounts of events and reporting results and highlights
composing a review of a film, story or documentary and expressing opinions about different perspectives
listening to extracts from expressive contemporary texts and identifying cultural elements
expressing responses to personal or peer experiences using evaluative and expressive language

AC9LS10C04.minimum_width: Translate a short familiar text and compare with another translation — identify at least two translation decisions and explain each; identify at least one word or expression where equivalence was not achievable.
AC9LS10C04.typical_width: Interpret and translate interactions and texts to convey meaning and intercultural understanding — comparing and reflecting on translation decisions, identifying culturally specific content that resists direct translation, evaluating online translation tools critically, creating bilingual texts for target language community audiences, and reflecting on miscommunication strategies.
wider: Translate a creative text (song, poem, advertisement) and annotate every decision point — explain where literal translation was abandoned and why
Evaluate an online translation of a target language text — identify every error, ambiguity or cultural loss, and explain what each reveals about the limits of machine translation
Create a bilingual text presenting Australian cultural content for a target language community audience — include a reflective note on the most challenging translation decisions made
elaborations: translating short familiar texts such as advertisements, songs or film clips, comparing own translation with others and analysing differences
reflecting on the difficulty of achieving equivalence in translations of creative texts
using, comparing and evaluating online translators for accuracy, efficiency and reliability
experimenting with translations of popular expressions or idioms, noticing when this creates potential for confusion
creating bilingual texts that present aspects of Australian culture for target language community audiences
considering how to maintain the integrity of original texts when translating culture-specific concepts and slang
reflecting on how meaning can be misinterpreted in intercultural interactions

AC9LS10C05.minimum_width: Create a text for a specific purpose and audience, selecting at least three vocabulary or structural choices deliberately — and explaining why each fits the purpose.
AC9LS10C05.typical_width: Create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts and purposes — using varied vocabulary, grammatical structures, features and conventions to engage different audiences. Create across formats: multimodal presentations, social media texts, journal entries, scripts for role-plays, speeches, narratives from multiple perspectives, and cultural ID profiles for target language community peers.
wider: Create texts on the same topic for two different audiences (e.g. a young learner of the target language and an adult target language speaker) — contrast the vocabulary, structure and convention choices made for each
Tell a story from three different points of view in the target language — using first, second and third person narration each with appropriate register and structural choices
Write a journal entry reflecting on a visit to a significant First Nations Country/Place — with permission referring to cultural knowledge of the site, and presenting in the target language
elaborations: creating a multimodal presentation comparing different perspectives on a topical issue
creating visual displays of data or information gathered from research to share with peers
composing different types of social media texts to present views on particular issues
writing a journal entry or contributing to a school newsletter reflecting on a visit to a significant First Nations Country/Place
writing the script for and presenting role-plays with characters and themes likely to appeal to specific audiences
composing and performing speeches or dialogues that reference significant celebrations or historical events
telling a story from several different perspectives and points of view
selecting images and writing descriptions from the perspective of different characters
composing a secure online cultural ID profile to exchange with target language community peers

AC9LS10U01.minimum_width: Apply pronunciation knowledge to read an unfamiliar text aloud with intelligible fluency; use intonation and tone to convey at least two different emotional meanings in spoken production.
AC9LS10U01.typical_width: Apply features and conventions of spoken target language to extend fluency — applying correct pronunciation to challenging combinations, using tone to convey emotion and modify meaning, applying intonation rhythm and pace in own spoken texts, experimenting with expressive range through read-aloud from unfamiliar texts, and using tongue twisters for pace and fluency.
wider: Apply expressive intonation to a range of emotionally varied texts — demonstrating command of tonal and prosodic variety beyond neutral statement delivery
Read aloud from a genuinely unfamiliar text (newspaper, novel extract, report) with adequate fluency and expressive range
Record own reading of a text and compare with a native speaker model — identify specific features to improve and explain the target
elaborations: applying correct pronunciation to challenging letter combinations in the target language
understanding how tone can convey emotions, modify meaning and give clues about what is happening
applying knowledge of pronunciation, intonation, rhythm and pace to own use of spoken target language
experimenting with intonation and stress, improving coherence and increasing expressive range by reading from unfamiliar texts
reciting tongue twisters to develop pace and fluency

AC9LS10U02.minimum_width: Use at least two complex grammatical structures correctly in a composition context (e.g. double negative, modelled subjunctive, conditional); use at least two cohesive devices beyond basic conjunctions.
AC9LS10U02.typical_width: Apply knowledge of grammatical structures to predict meaning and compose texts with some complex structures — including indefinite adjectives/pronouns, double negatives, reflexive verbs, modelled subjunctive, conditional, complex cohesive devices, verb conjugation across a range of tenses, passive/impersonal structures, acronyms and abbreviations, and imperative forms for varied purposes.
wider: Compose a text that uses modelled subjunctive, conditional and imperative forms each at least once — explaining the purpose of each in a margin note
Identify all grammatically complex structures in a given target language text — categorise by type and explain the function of each in context
Compose a text that deliberately uses passive or impersonal structures where an active equivalent would be possible — explain why the impersonal was the better choice
elaborations: understanding and using indefinite adjectives and pronouns
applying constructions with double negation
understanding the difference between a reflexive verb and the corresponding non-reflexive verb
using modelled subjunctive mood to express doubt, uncertainty or emotion
expressing hypothetical events using modelled conditional voice structures
using cohesive devices to extend sentence complexity and sophistication
conjugating verbs to describe a range of events across time
extending understanding of symbols, acronyms, abbreviations and colloquial shortenings
recognising the different usage of imperative forms
using numbers for a range of purposes including historical and biographical timelines
using the passive, impersonal form

AC9LS10U03.minimum_width: Use metalanguage to analyse at least two language features in a target language text — naming the feature, describing its function, and explaining the effect it creates.
AC9LS10U03.typical_width: Reflect on and evaluate target language texts using metalanguage — developing vocabulary for complex grammatical features, analysing how language creates effects in different text types, identifying common textual conventions, comparing features and functions across text types, and reflecting on spoken versus written differences.
wider: Analyse two target language texts of different types (e.g. a drama and a news bulletin) using the same metalanguage framework — compare how each text type uses language to create its intended effect
Evaluate a political or persuasive target language text — use metalanguage to identify every rhetorical strategy and explain what effect each is designed to create

Create a glossary of metalanguage for complex target language features — including subjunctive, conditional, reflexive and impersonal — each with a definition, example and explanation of when it is used
elaborations: developing metalanguage to extend discussion of grammatical features such as word order, tenses and subjunctive mood
analysing and comparing different types of texts to demonstrate how language is used to create effects
identifying common textual conventions in different text types
identifying key features and functions that characterise different types of texts and reflecting on how these are used for effect
comparing the features and differences of spoken and written texts

AC9LS10U04.minimum_width: Reflect on at least one personal experience of the target language and culture — identifying a specific challenge or insight; explain how at least one language variation feature reflects cultural or social identity.
AC9LS10U04.typical_width: Reflect on and evaluate how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — sharing personal learning reflections, recognising differences in communicative norms between the target language and English, understanding how language variation signals identity and inclusion/exclusion, reflecting on First Nations Australian acknowledgement protocols, exploring co-official language debates, and examining how proverbs and word choices reflect cultural attitudes.
wider: Examine the use of language to include or exclude in target language community contexts — find examples of jargon, slang or political language that signal in-group membership and explain the social mechanism
Evaluate current debates around a hybrid language variety in the target language community — explain what each position reveals about cultural identity, ownership and linguistic change

Research the protocols for authentically co-creating an Acknowledgement of Country with a First Nations Australian — reflect on what this process reveals about the difference between cultural acknowledgement and cultural performance
elaborations: sharing reflections on experiences of learning the target language and on reactions to aspects of the language and culture
recognising differences in the nature and function of some elements of communication in the target language compared with English
understanding how language variation can reflect cultural and social identity, and inclusion or exclusion
reflecting on the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place with a First Nations Australian, to present in the target language
researching co-official target languages and investigating the history and issues surrounding such language relationships
reflecting on the development of hybrid language varieties in target language communities and evaluating debates around them
examining the meaning of proverbs and how they reflect historical cultural views and attitudes
exploring how word choices can indicate attitudes and values
comparing texts created for different audiences in different target language communities, noticing how language reflects priorities and values
